items.pronunciation_notes: Unaspirated k — no puff of air at all. The English k of 'kite' is aspirated and comes out as ख; the k inside 'skate' is the right sound.

learn.title_en: क — the k with no breath
learn.explanation_en: क is made at the back of the mouth like an English k, but with no puff of air after it. English aspirates its k at the start of a word, so reading क as in 'kite' produces ख instead; the k inside 'skate' is exactly right. Remember from Module 1 that every consonant also carries an unwritten अ, so this letter on its own is read 'ka', not 'k'.

examples.note: Opens with a clean क, and the final vowel is not pronounced.
क carrying the long ा matra you learned in Module 1.
क at the end of a word, where its अ disappears entirely.

common_error.why_en: Adding English's automatic puff of breath turns क into ख, which is a different letter.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which letter makes the sound at the start of this word?
practice.question: कमल
practice.explanation_en: The sound is voiceless and releases no breath, which makes it क rather than ख.

game.question_en: Which word begins with an aspirated consonant — one released with a puff of air?
game.explanation_en: खाना starts with ख, which carries the puff. The other three start with क, said with no breath at all.

items.pronunciation_notes: क with a clear puff of breath released after it — roughly the k of English 'kite'. Not the scraping ch of German 'Bach', which is the separate letter ख़.

learn.explanation_en: ख is exactly क with a strong puff of breath released after it. English speakers already make this sound at the start of words like 'kite' and 'cool', so producing it is easy — the discipline is using it only where ख is actually written. Do not reach for the scraping sound of German 'Bach'; that belongs to a different letter taught much later.

examples.note: A word you will use daily, and the puff is unmistakable.
Compare कोना, 'corner', from Module 1 — the two words are one puff apart.
The breath is released in the middle of the word, on ख.

common_error.why_en: Without the puff of breath the verb 'to lose' collapses into the noun 'corner'.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which letter makes the sound at the start of this word?
practice.question: खाना
practice.explanation_en: The sound is voiceless and followed by a clear puff, which makes it ख and not क.

game.question_en: Which word begins with an aspirated consonant?
game.explanation_en: खोना begins with ख. The other three begin with क, which releases no breath.

items.pronunciation_notes: Voiced g as in 'go', with no puff of air. Unlike क, the vocal cords are already buzzing as the sound is released.

learn.title_en: ग — the voiced partner of क
learn.explanation_en: ग is the g of English 'go'. It is made in the same place as क; the difference is voicing, meaning your vocal cords are running as the sound is released. English g is never aspirated, so this letter causes English speakers almost no trouble. The shape of every sound family is now visible: a voiceless pair and a voiced pair, each with a plain and a breathy member.

examples.note: Clean voiced g, then the long ा matra.
Two syllables, and the final vowel drops as usual.
ग at the end of a word.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which letter makes the sound at the start of this word?
practice.question: गाना
practice.explanation_en: The sound is voiced but releases no breath, which makes it ग and not घ.

game.question_en: Which word begins with an aspirated consonant?
game.explanation_en: घर begins with घ, which is voiced and released with breath. The other three begin with plain ग.

summary.recap_en: This level opened the क-family with क, ख and ग, and set up the grid every sound family follows: voiceless against voiced, each with a plain and an aspirated member.
summary.next_up_en: Next: घ and ङ complete the family, followed by a drill on the क/ख contrast.

items.pronunciation_notes: Voiced g released with breath — a murmured sound English has no equivalent for. It is one consonant, not g followed by a separate h.

learn.title_en: घ — voiced and breathy at once
learn.explanation_en: घ is ग released with breath, something English never does: the voicing and the puff happen together, giving the sound a murmured quality. Do not produce it as two separate sounds. A reliable trick is to start from a sigh and let the g emerge out of it. This letter arrives early and stays, because घर, 'house', is one of the most common nouns in the language.

examples.note: The single most useful word containing this letter.
The same breathy release, followed by a long ा.
Breathy घ at the start, and the dot read as ṇ because ट follows.

common_error.why_en: Dropping the breath gives plain ग, and a listener hears a different word.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which letter makes the sound at the start of this word?
practice.question: घर
practice.explanation_en: The sound is voiced and carries breath at the same time, which is घ and not ग.

game.question_en: Which word begins with an aspirated consonant?
game.explanation_en: घास begins with घ, which is released with breath. The other three begin with plain ग.

items.pronunciation_notes: The ng of English 'sing'. The full letter is almost never written in modern Hindi — the sound is spelt with the anusvara ं before a क-family consonant.

learn.title_en: ङ — the sound you know, the letter you rarely see
learn.explanation_en: ङ is the ng of English 'sing' and 'thank'. Every sound family has a nasal of its own, and this is the क-family's. You will hardly ever meet the full letter: modern Hindi writes the anusvara ं instead, and the dot takes its colour from whatever consonant follows. In रंग the dot is read as ng precisely because ग comes after it.

examples.note: The dot is read ng here because a क-family letter follows it.
Again the dot before ग is pronounced ng, not n.
The nasal appears before घ, another member of the same family.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which sound does the dot stand for in this word?
practice.question: रंग
practice.explanation_en: A क-family consonant follows, so the dot is pronounced as the velar nasal ङ — the ng of 'sing'.

game.question_en: In which of these words is the nasal followed by an aspirated consonant?
game.explanation_en: कंघी has घ after the nasal, which is released with breath. The others have plain ग or क.

items.pronunciation_notes: The only difference is the puff of breath. Test it with a strip of paper held in front of your mouth: क leaves it still, ख makes it jump.

learn.explanation_en: This is the contrast Module 1 introduced, now with letters attached to it. English chooses aspiration automatically by position — puffed at the start of a word, plain after s — so an English speaker reading कान will almost certainly produce खान. The fix is mechanical rather than musical: hold a strip of paper in front of your mouth and keep it perfectly still for क.

examples.note: No breath. The paper does not move.
One puff of air, and the word has changed completely.
A very common word where the puff must not appear.

common_error.why_en: Meaning 'ear', but importing English's automatic puff produces the word for a mine.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which letter makes the sound at the start of this word?
practice.question: कान
practice.explanation_en: Nothing is released after the sound, so it is क — कान, meaning 'ear'.

game.question_en: Which word begins with an aspirated consonant?
game.explanation_en: खान begins with ख and releases a puff of air. The other three begin with the plain क.

summary.recap_en: This level closed the क-family with घ and ङ, and drilled the क/ख contrast — a mistake English speakers make out of habit rather than ignorance, since they can already produce both sounds.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the च-family, where the same four-way grid repeats one step forward in the mouth.

items.pronunciation_notes: Unaspirated ch — lighter than the ch of English 'church', which is aspirated and comes out as छ. Written 'ch' here; the doubled 'chh' marks its aspirated partner.

learn.explanation_en: च is made just behind the teeth ridge, close to the ch of English 'church' but without the puff of air English adds. The grid from the क-family repeats exactly here: च voiceless and plain, छ voiceless and breathy, ज voiced and plain, झ voiced and breathy. If your ch comes out forceful, you are producing छ.

examples.note: The word you will say most often in India — keep it light.
Plain च with no breath released after it.
The final vowel of न drops, as it always does.

common_error.why_en: English's forceful ch adds breath and turns च into छ, a separate letter.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which letter makes the sound at the start of this word?
practice.question: चाय
practice.explanation_en: The sound is voiceless and light, with no breath after it, so it is च.

game.question_en: Which word begins with an aspirated consonant?
game.explanation_en: छह begins with छ, which carries a puff of air. The other three begin with the light च.

items.pronunciation_notes: च with a strong puff of breath — close to the ch of English 'cheese' said emphatically. The doubled h marks aspiration, not a longer sound.

learn.explanation_en: छ is च released with a clear puff of air. English speakers can already make it, since the ch at the start of 'cheese' is close, so the work is the same as with क and ख: use it only where it is written. Handwritten छ and ख look alike to beginners, so read the whole word before deciding which one you are looking at.

examples.note: A number you will need constantly.
Aspirated छ, then the retroflex ट arriving in level five.
The puff is released in the middle of the word.

common_error.why_en: Without the puff of breath छ becomes च, and the spelling no longer matches any word.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which letter makes the sound at the start of this word?
practice.question: छोटा
practice.explanation_en: A clear puff follows the sound, which makes it छ rather than the light च.

game.question_en: Which word begins with an aspirated consonant?
game.explanation_en: छोटा begins with छ, released with breath. The other three begin with the plain च.

items.pronunciation_notes: The j of English 'jam', voiced and with no puff. Its dotted form ज़, pronounced z, is a separate letter taught in level thirteen.

learn.explanation_en: ज is the j of English 'jam'. It occupies the voiced and plain slot of the च-family, exactly where ग sits in the क-family. English j is never aspirated, so this letter is easy. One warning: adding a dot underneath produces ज़, pronounced z, which is a separate letter with its own set of words — the two are not spelling variants of each other.

examples.note: Plain voiced j at the start of one of the commonest verbs.
The ह at the end is lightly pronounced rather than dropped.
ज at the end of a word.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which letter makes the sound at the start of this word?
practice.question: जाना
practice.explanation_en: The sound is voiced but releases no breath, which makes it ज and not झ.

game.question_en: Which word begins with an aspirated consonant?
game.explanation_en: झूठ begins with झ, which is voiced and breathy at once. The other three begin with plain ज.

summary.recap_en: This level opened the च-family with च, छ and ज, and showed that every sound family repeats the same four-way grid: voiceless plain, voiceless breathy, voiced plain, voiced breathy.
summary.next_up_en: Next: झ and ञ close the family, followed by a drill on the च/छ contrast.

items.pronunciation_notes: Voiced j released with breath, murmured in the same way as घ. It is one sound, not j followed by h.

learn.explanation_en: झ stands to ज exactly as घ stands to ग: the same sound, released with breath while the voicing continues underneath. English has no consonant like this, so build it the same way you built घ — start from a sigh and let the j emerge out of it. Produce it as two separate sounds and a Hindi listener hears ज followed by ह.

examples.note: Breathy झ, a long ऊ, then a retroflex arriving next level.
The dot before ड is read as the retroflex nasal.
The breathy release sits in the middle of a very common verb.

common_error.why_en: Dropping the breath gives ज, and जूठ is a real but quite different word, used of food someone has already eaten from.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which letter makes the sound at the start of this word?
practice.question: झूठ
practice.explanation_en: The sound is voiced and carries breath at the same time, which is झ and not ज.

game.question_en: Which word begins with an aspirated consonant?
game.explanation_en: झंडा begins with झ, released with breath. The other three begin with the plain ज.

items.pronunciation_notes: The ny of English 'canyon'. Like ङ it is almost never written as a full letter — the anusvara ं carries the sound before a च-family consonant.

learn.title_en: ञ — the nasal you spell with a dot
learn.explanation_en: ञ is the ny of English 'canyon' and 'onion'. It is the च-family's nasal, and like ङ it survives as a sound rather than a written letter: modern Hindi writes the anusvara ं and lets the following consonant decide how the dot is read. Before च, छ, ज or झ, that dot is ञ.

examples.note: The dot before च is read as ny.
Same rule — a च-family letter follows, so the nasal is ñ.
Before ज the dot is again the palatal nasal.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which sound does the dot stand for in this word?
practice.question: चंचल
practice.explanation_en: A च-family consonant follows, so the dot is read as the palatal nasal ञ — the ny of 'canyon'.

game.question_en: Which word begins with an aspirated consonant?
game.explanation_en: छाता begins with छ, which releases a puff of air. The other three begin with unaspirated consonants.

items.pronunciation_notes: The two differ only by the puff of breath. English speakers over-aspirate at the start of a word, so च is the letter that needs the practice, not छ.

learn.explanation_en: This is the same aspiration problem as क and ख, moved forward in the mouth. English speakers make the aspirated छ automatically at the start of a word and then have to unlearn it for च. The pair repays real drilling because both letters are frequent: चल is the everyday 'go on, come on', while छल means deceit.

examples.note: No breath at all — the paper in front of your mouth stays still.
One puff, and the meaning is unrecognisable.
The commonest word with this letter. Keep it light.

common_error.why_en: Meaning 'come on', but English's automatic puff of breath produces the noun for deceit.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which letter makes the sound at the start of this word?
practice.question: चल
practice.explanation_en: Nothing is released after the sound, so it is च — चल, meaning 'come on'.

game.question_en: Which word begins with an aspirated consonant?
game.explanation_en: छल begins with छ and releases a puff of air. The other three begin with the plain च.

summary.recap_en: This level closed the च-family with झ and ञ, and drilled the च/छ contrast — the same aspiration habit that made क and ख difficult, one step forward in the mouth.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the retroflex family opens with ट, ठ and ड — sounds English has no letters for at all.

items.pronunciation_notes: Tongue tip curled back to touch the roof of the mouth, with no puff of air. The t of English 'stop' is closest in breath, though it is made further forward.

learn.explanation_en: For ट the tip of the tongue curls up and back to touch the roof of the mouth, well behind the teeth. English has no letter for this, but English speakers produce something close to it every time they say a t, which is exactly why the दाल and डाल confusion from Module 1 happens. Here the difficulty is reversed: ट is the sound your mouth already wants to make, so this letter is the easy one and त, arriving in level seven, will be the hard one.

examples.note: Both t sounds are retroflex, whatever the English spelling suggests.
Curl the tongue back before the ओ.
The retroflex sits in the middle, after the aspirated छ from last level.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which letter makes the sound at the start of this word?
practice.question: टोपी
practice.explanation_en: The tongue curls back and nothing is released after the sound, so it is ट.

game.question_en: Which word begins with an aspirated consonant?
game.explanation_en: ठंडा begins with ठ, which adds a puff of air to the retroflex. The other three begin with plain ट.

items.pronunciation_notes: ट with a puff of breath. The h marks aspiration, not the th of English 'think' or 'this' — neither of those sounds exists in Hindi.

learn.explanation_en: ठ is ट released with a puff of air. The transliteration misleads badly: English speakers see th and reach for the sound in 'think' or 'this', and neither exists anywhere in Hindi. Keep the tongue curled back at the roof of the mouth and simply add breath to what you already do for ट.

examples.note: The dot before ड is read as the retroflex nasal.
One of the most frequent words in everyday conversation.
The aspirated retroflex falls in the middle of the word.

common_error.why_en: Without the puff of breath ठ becomes ट, which is a different letter.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which letter makes the sound at the start of this word?
practice.question: ठंडा
practice.explanation_en: The tongue is curled back and a puff of air follows, which makes it ठ — not the dental द and not the plain ट.

game.question_en: Which word begins with an aspirated consonant?
game.explanation_en: ठीक begins with ठ, the retroflex released with breath. The other three begin with plain ट.

items.pronunciation_notes: The voiced retroflex — tongue curled back, vocal cords running, no puff. Its dotted form ड़ is a flapped sound and a separate letter, taught in level fifteen.

learn.explanation_en: ड is ट with the vocal cords running: tongue curled back, no breath released. This is the letter behind the दाल and डाल confusion from Module 1, and the one an English d turns into by default. Adding a dot underneath gives ड़, a flapped sound made by flicking the tongue forward, which is a separate letter with its own words.

examples.note: Retroflex — compare दाल, 'lentils', where the tongue touches the teeth.
One syllable; the final vowel drops.
The dot before ड is read as the retroflex nasal ṇ.

common_error.why_en: Meaning 'branch', but putting the tongue on the teeth gives the dental द and the word for lentils.

practice.prompt_en: Listen. Which letter makes the sound at the start of this word?
practice.question: डर
practice.explanation_en: The tongue curls back and no breath follows, so it is the retroflex ड and not the dental द.

game.question_en: Which word begins with an aspirated consonant?
game.explanation_en: ढाई begins with ढ, the voiced retroflex released with breath. The other three begin with plain ड.

summary.recap_en: This level opened the retroflex family with ट, ठ and ड — sounds English has no letters for, even though English speakers produce something close to them every time they say a t or a d.
summary.next_up_en: Next: ढ and ण complete the retroflex family, followed by the drill that separates the whole series from the dental one.
